data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible without induction because it functions as a pragmatic wager: while past success guarantees nothing about the future, choosing the theory that has demonstrated 'fitness' by surviving severe tests is the only rational choice available if one must act.","counterconditions":[{"case":"refuted if it can be demonstrated that preferring the better-corroborated theory logically entails an assumption that the future will resemble the past, thereby making the 'pragmatic wager' indistinguishable from the inductive principle Popper explicitly rejects","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if the very act of selecting a theory based on past survival implicitly assumes that past performance is a reliable indicator of future utility","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if the analogy of betting on a horse fails because, unlike a horse race, scientific theories face an unknown reality where survival demonstrates no positive 'fitness'","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"refuted if the phrase 'educated guesswork' is a contradiction in terms within a strictly non-inductive framework, rendering the preference an arbitrary psychological habit","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between epistemic probability (which Popper rejects as increased by corroboration) and pragmatic rationality. It argues that acting on the best-tested theory is akin to betting on a horse that has won every race; the agent does not believe the horse will win (no inductive leap), but recognizes it as the unique rational option given the constraint of necessary action.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
